actions.before: Er-jie took two dishes of food, ordered a large cup filled with wine, and told Xing-er to squat at the foot of the kang and eat. She kept up a stream of questions: how old was his mistress at home, how was she so formidable, how old were the old lady and Her Ladyship, how many young ladies were there? She asked about every sort of household matter. Grinning as he ate below the edge of the kang, Xing-er gave mother and daughters a detailed account of the Rong mansion.

actions.before: Xing-er clapped his hands and laughed.
actions.after: Joker clapped his hands and laughed.

actions.before: ‘A rose is red and fragrant,’ Xing-er said with a grin. ‘Who doesn't love it? Only its thorns prick your hand. She's another formidable spirit. It's a pity Her Ladyship didn't bear her: a phoenix out of a crow's nest! The fourth is still little. She's actually Master Zhen's own sister. She's been motherless since she was little, so the old lady told Her Ladyship to take her over and bring her up. She's another who won't interfere in anything. You don't know, ma'am, but apart from our own young ladies there are two more, rare even in Heaven and without equal on earth. One is Miss Lin, the daughter of our master's aunt. Her little name is Dai-yu or something. Her face and figure are not unlike Third Aunt's. She's full of literary learning, but ill from head to foot. Even in weather like this she wears lined clothes. She only has to come out for the wind to knock her over. Those lawless mouths of ours call her “the Ailing Xi Shi” behind her back. The other is Her Ladyship's sister's daughter, Miss Xue, called Bao-chai. She looks as if she'd been heaped together out of snow.

decisions.reason: Lady Xing is unmistakably Xi-feng’s own mother-in-law, contrasted with the old lady and Her Ladyship whom Joker says Xi-feng flatters. The whole accusation and quoted black-hen complaint remain Joker’s reported speech, not narrator certification. This is clarity, not a claim that the prior relationship was false.

actions.finding: The appositive senior Lady Jia is a recoverable marital-title rendering of 大太太, not a wrong mother-in-law, but it reads like a new name beside established Lady Xing and Grandmother Jia. Using Lady Xing restores immediately recognizable identity. This does not turn the page’s reported complaint into narrator fact.
actions.before: ‘If any of us has done something wrong, the mistress won't let it pass. We only have to beg Miss Patience, and it's settled. Nowadays there isn't a soul in the whole household, high or low, who doesn't hate our mistress, except the old lady and Her Ladyship. People only keep up appearances because they're afraid of her. She never thinks anyone else as good as herself. All she cares about is keeping those two ladies pleased. If she says one, it's one; if she says two, it's two. No one dares stand in her way. She'd like to save every scrap of silver and copper and pile it into a mountain, so the old lady and Her Ladyship will say how well she manages. What they don't see is that the servants suffer and she gets the credit. If there's anything good in the offing, she won't wait for someone else to mention it: she pushes herself to the front. If there's trouble, or she's made a mistake herself, she ducks her head and pushes it onto someone else, then stands by fanning the flames. Even her own mother-in-law, the senior Lady Jia, is disgusted with her now. “A sparrow flies to the flourishing branch,” she says. “Black hens stick to their own nest! Neglecting her own affairs to bustle about blindly for other people!”
